lines: Week six: token classification. Every token gets its own label, and we read structure back from the labels.
Ada visits Paris. For parts of speech: proper noun, verb, proper noun, punctuation.
For named entities: B person, outside, B location, outside. Same tokens, two different tasks.
Why is this harder than labeling a whole text? The labels must fit together, entities have boundaries, and they are judged as spans.
B I O has rules. I must continue a span of the same type.
O followed by I person is invalid: there is no person to continue. B organization followed by I person is invalid: the type changes.
But B person, B person is valid: two people standing next to each other.
One flat B I O layer cannot hold nested entities, like a location inside a university name.
The same output shape solves many tasks. The task is defined by what the label means.
Chunking marks phrases: B noun phrase, I noun phrase. Inside a noun phrase can be an adjective.
Slot filling: fly from Boston to Paris. Boston is the departure, Paris is the arrival, although both are places.
Punctuation restoration labels what to insert after each word. And Turkish evlerden needs a whole bundle: noun, plural, ablative.
A transformer splits words into subword pieces, so the labels must be aligned.
Ada and Washington, two people. Washington becomes wash plus ington.
With the first-piece policy, the first piece of each word gets the word's label. Everything else gets minus one hundred.
Minus one hundred means ignore this position in the loss. O is different: it is a real label that the model learns.
Now evaluation. A hundred tokens: ninety outside, ten inside entities.
Predict outside everywhere and you get ninety percent accuracy, but you found zero entities.
So entities are scored as exact spans: the same boundaries and the same type.
Gold: Ada, and New York. The prediction finds Ada, and only York.
York has the right type but the wrong boundary. It is one false positive, and New York is one false negative.
One true positive, one false positive, one false negative: F1 is two over four, one half.
